panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A captioned as chancroid with serpiginous undermined non-infiltrating ulcers, dirty bottom, and unilateral inflammatory inguinal lymphadenopathy; image shows ulcer at penile base and swollen inguinal bubo. B: Panel B captioned as ulcers by reinoculation (in-text cerco ulcers from self-inoculation) of chancroid; image shows genital ulcer plus satellite reinoculation ulcer circled in red.
panels.attribution_text: Cunha Ramos et al. Genital ulcers caused by sexually transmitted agents.. Anais brasileiros de dermatologia 2022. doi:10.1016/j.abd.2022.01.004. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 9.
panels.figure_caption: (A), Chancroid: non-infiltrating, serpiginous and undermined ulcers. “Dirty” bottom and painful, usually unilateral, inflammatory inguinal lymphadenopathy. (B), Ulcers by reinoculation. Clinical pictures belong to Prof. Sinésio Talhari private collection.
in_text_mentions: These can cause vaginal or anal discharge or bleeding. They quickly develop into pustules that, when they rupture, originate ulcers whose edges are described as irregular, serpiginous and undermined (Fig. 9a). The bottom of the ulceration is often friable and covered by pyonecrotic exudate. The base does not show infiltration, except in the case of secondary infection. Self-inoculation results in the so-called “cerco ulcers” (Fig. 9b), as well as ulcers in the fold areas, described as “in book pages”. As a complication, gangrene in extensive areas of the skin or even penile gangrene may occur.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A shows lesions over the knee in Haemophilus ducreyi cutaneous ulcer outbreak; article title and caption attribute cutaneous ulcers to H. ducreyi. Extragenital cutaneous form is variant of chancroid. Ulcer morphology closest to soft-chancre ulcer vocabulary. B: Panel-specific caption attributes below-knee lesions to H. ducreyi outbreak; visible ulcers with irregular borders support chancroid ulcer morphology in extragenital site. C: Panel-specific caption attributes mid-lateral leg lesion to H. ducreyi; visible ulcer with irregular border and crusted base matches described 'base of the ulcer was mostly composed of dry and crusted tissue'. D: Panel-specific caption attributes ankle lesion to H. ducreyi; visible ulcer with irregular border supports chancroid ulcer morphology in extragenital site.

in_text_mentions: A swab was taken and sent for culture, including an exudate smear from the wound margin for Diff-Quik staining. In the smear, we saw small rod-shaped bacteria (Fig 3). Culture of the wound was performed according to standard laboratory procedures. After 48 hours of incubation (5% CO2 at 37°C), growth of small grey colonies was observed on the chocolate agar plate (PolyViteX, bioMérieux Marcy l'Etoile, France) (Fig 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A lateral view of painful indurated malleolar ulcer with undermined margins in Haemophilus ducreyi cutaneous ulcer article; morphology matches undermined chancroid ulcer but at extragenital cutaneous site, hence variant extragenital presentation. B: Panel B dorsal view of same right lateral malleolar ulcer described in caption with undermined margins; Haemophilus ducreyi cutaneous ulcer per article title, extragenital variant of chancroid.

in_text_mentions: e was referred to the Center of Tropical Medicine and Travel Medicine of the Academic Medical Center (AMC) in Amsterdam. Upon physical examination, he appeared healthy with a normal blood pressure and body temperature. On the right lateral malleolus, we saw an indurated ulcer of 3 × 3 cm with a hypergranulomatous surface, perilesional erythema and oedema, and undermined wound margins (Fig 2). The ulcer was very painful upon manipulation. There was no evidence of regional adenopathy. All laboratory results were normal, including a white blood cell count of 8.4 × 109/L (normal 4 − 10.5 × 109/L).
